terms.definition: Football Outsiders' run-blocking measure that credits the offensive line more for short gains and losses and less for long runs.
The average distance downfield of a quarterback's targets, in air yards.
terms.variants: NGS: 'Average Intended Air Yards' and 'Average Targeted Air Yards'.

terms.definition: The distance a pass travels downfield in the air, measured from the line of scrimmage to where it is caught or aimed.
A certified athletic trainer in the stadium booth who watches for injuries and can call for a player to be examined.
An offense starting a possession or a down near its own goal line, with little room behind it.
The sideline zone behind the white border where a team's players, coaches and staff stand, with only credentialed people allowed.
The share of dropbacks on which the defense blitzes, meaning it rushes more players than usual.
Up to six players per team (active, inactive or honorary) named before kickoff to take part in the coin toss and speak for the team.
A one-way radio that lets a coach talk to one offensive player and one defensive player through a helmet speaker until the play clock hits 15 seconds or the snap.
The elevated room where assistant coaches and analysts watch the game and pass information to the sideline.
The NFL's procedure for a player hit in the head: removal for a sideline exam by team physician and UNC with video review, then locker-room exam if symptoms appear.
A quarterback's actual completion rate minus the rate expected from the difficulty of his throws (depth, separation, pressure and so on).
terms.variants: NFL Next Gen Stats calls it 'Completion Percentage Above Expectation'.

terms.definition: The stretch of the opponent's half that is too far for a reliable field goal yet too close for a punt to gain much, so teams often go for it on fourth down.
terms.variants: College range can run from about the opponent's 33 to 43; shrinks as NFL kickers improve. 'Fringe' is the draft's name; sources say dead zone or four-down territory.

terms.definition: The team that wins the opening coin toss waits until the second half to choose between receiving or kicking and which goal to defend.
The share of drives on which the offense either gains a first down or scores.
Football Outsiders' rating of how much better or worse a team or unit is than league average on each play, adjusted for down and distance and opponent strength.
A player's total value above a replacement-level player, expressed in yards, over a season rather than per play.
terms.variants: Earlier called DPAR (points).

terms.definition: The average points the team with the ball can expect to score next, given down, distance, field position and time remaining.
terms.variants: ESPN's scale runs from about minus 3 to 7.

terms.definition: The change in expected points from the start of a play to the start of the next, used to value each play.
A run or pass that gains a large chunk of yards; the cutoff varies (commonly 10 or more on runs, 15 or more on passes).
terms.variants: 4for4: 10+ rush, 15+ pass. Sumer: 15+ pass. PFF 'breakaway' run: 15+. College Football Data uses 'explosiveness' to mean average PPA on successful plays, a different measure.

terms.definition: The usual first-down situation: a new series of four downs where the line to gain is 10 yards from the snap spot.
The strategy of plays a team prepares to beat the opponent it is about to face.
The late stretch of a game that is already decided, whose yards and points are weighted less in analytics.
Using a fourth down for a run or pass to get a first down instead of punting or kicking a field goal.
The share of defensive plays that end in a tackle for loss, forced fumble, pass breakup or similar disruption.
A pass rush that does not finish in a sack but makes the quarterback throw early or move before he wants to.

terms.term: Intentional fouls to manipulate the clock
terms.definition: Committing several fouls on one down to run time off the clock is itself a foul, costing 15 yards and resetting the clock to the snap.
A team lets the other side score a safety on purpose, for example to run the clock out or avoid a risky punt from its own end zone.
A play where the quarterback takes the snap and kneels to end the play and keep the clock running, used by a leading team to run out the clock.
terms.variants: victory formation

terms.definition: A play where the quarterback takes the snap and kneels, ending the play at once with little risk so the clock keeps running.

aliases: net yards gained per passing attempt
terms.definition: Passing yards minus sack yards, divided by pass attempts plus sacks.
terms.variants: ANY/A adds 20 yards per touchdown and subtracts 45 per interception.

terms.definition: An offense that lines up and snaps the ball without a full huddle, to save time or to catch the defense before it can substitute.
terms.variants: Wikipedia separates the hurry-up no-huddle (HUNH) style from the two-minute drill, which is the clock-driven version.

terms.definition: Rushing yards gained more than 10 yards past the line of scrimmage.
A separate coin toss at the start of overtime; the winner chooses between receiving or kicking and which goal to defend.
A down with enough yardage to go that the offense is expected to pass: second-and-7 or 8 and longer, or third or fourth down with 5 or more yards.
terms.variants: FSH: second-and-7+; CFBD: second-and-8+.

aliases: extra down at end of period
terms.definition: One extra untimed down given at the end of a period or half when the defense commits an accepted live-ball foul on the last play, among other cases.
Points scored divided by the number of drives.
terms.variants: 4for4 leaves out drives that end in kneel-downs.

terms.definition: The share of runs on third or fourth down with two or fewer yards to go that get a first down or touchdown.
The elevated media area of the stadium, where reporters and broadcasters work.
The share of a quarterback's dropbacks on which the defense hurries, hits or sacks him.
terms.variants: PFF defines 'under pressure' as any time the passer is disturbed from his normal throwing motion.

terms.definition: How much more (or less) often a team passes than a model expects for the situation.
The stretch of field from the defense's 20-yard line to its goal line, used mainly to track how well offenses finish drives.
The share of a team's trips inside the 20 that end in a touchdown.
The baseline of what a freely available bench-level player would produce, against which players are measured.
How often a quarterback's dropbacks end in a sack.
Second down with a lot of yardage still needed for the line to gain; analytics sources set the cutoff at 7 or 8 yards.
terms.variants: Football Study Hall counts 'second-and-7 or more' as a passing down; College Football Data counts 'second-and-8 or longer'.

terms.definition: Second down needing only a few yards; analytics sources class second down as a standard down when seven or fewer yards remain.
Rushing yards gained between 5 and 10 yards past the line of scrimmage.
The four consecutive downs an offense gets to reach the line to gain, starting at first down.
A down where only a yard or two is needed for a first down or touchdown, usually met with power runs.
The NFL's team-sideline system (now Microsoft Surface PCs) that lets coaches and players review plays and data instead of the old paper photos.
The numbers and coded words called by the quarterback in the huddle or at the line of scrimmage before each play; defenses call them too, usually through a linebacker.
The solid white band six feet wide around the field; only officials may stand inside it while play is on.
The number of plays a player is on the field, counted as snaps; contracts and rules use percentages of a team's snaps.
The quarterback immediately throws the ball into the ground after the snap to stop the clock, at the cost of a down.
A down where the distance is manageable (first down, or second-and-7 or fewer, third-and-4 or fewer) so the offense may run or pass.
terms.variants: College Football Data: passing downs are second-and-8+ and third or fourth-and-5+; everything else is standard.

terms.definition: The share of runs stopped at or behind the line of scrimmage.
The share of plays judged successful; the test differs by publisher (positive EPA, or gaining a set share of the needed yards).
terms.variants: Football Outsiders style: 40% of needed yards on first down, 60% on second, 100% on third or fourth. Sumer and 4for4: positive EPA.

terms.definition: A pass thrown toward a given receiver, counted whether or not it is caught.
After the two-minute warning, certain clock-saving acts by the offense (or some replay and nullified-foul cases) cost 10 seconds off the game clock; the offense may burn a timeout instead.
Third down with many yards to go, where a conversion usually needs a pass; analytics sources start the passing-down label at about five yards.
Third down needing only about a yard or two, where one play can move the chains.
A drive that ends in a punt after three plays without a first down.
terms.variants: Canadian football: 'two and out'.

terms.definition: How long each team holds the ball; the two shares add up to the game's playing time.
Seconds from the snap to the release of a pass, averaged over attempts (sacks left out in Next Gen Stats).
terms.variants: PFF's closest stat is 'time in pocket', described as snap to throw.

terms.definition: Each NFL team gets three charged timeouts in each half, and two in a regular-season overtime period.
terms.variants: Postseason overtime: three per half of overtime.

terms.definition: A team's or player's rushing yards plus passing yards (in the NFL, less sack yards for the passer).
ESPN's 0-100 quarterback rating built from every play's expected points added, giving the quarterback credit for passes, runs, sacks, turnovers and penalties.
The offense loses the ball to the defense by interception or fumble.
terms.variants: Wikipedia also uses 'turnover' loosely for a turnover on downs.

aliases: turn the ball over on downs
terms.definition: The offense uses all four downs without a first down or score, and the other team takes the ball where the last play ended.
An automatic timeout in the second and fourth quarters when the clock reaches two minutes (after the play in progress).
terms.variants: The NCAA has called its version the two-minute timeout since 2024.

terms.definition: An estimate of a team's chance to win at a given game state, built from how teams in the same spot did historically.
How much a play changed a team's chance to win, from before to after the play.
Receiving yards divided by the number of pass routes the player ran.
A solid yellow line six feet behind the white border in the bench area; players (except one charting the game) stay behind it, leaving the strip for coaches.
terms.variants: A broken yellow line also runs along the sideline outside the bench areas.
